body.text: On October 29, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets took a risk none of his colleagues have since Russia's full-scale invasion: he entered enemy territory.
Under a humanitarian deal brokered by the US's first lady, Melania Trump, he embarked on a three-day mission through Belarus, Russia and occupied Ukraine to evacuate a terrorised frontline city.
Oleshky, which sits on the southern side of the Dnipro River, has been under occupation since the first day of Russia's invasion in February 2022.
Moscow has used the strategic location as a launch pad for attacks. Kyiv says its neighbour has been exploiting the trapped local residents, using them as human shields.
The humanitarian situation there rapidly deteriorated over the past year with months'-long food and medical shortages for the roughly 2,000 trapped residents.
As fears of starvation set in, Ms Trump managed to do something her husband, US President Donald Trump, has not: negotiate a localised ceasefire with the Kremlin.

"She used her own opportunities to discuss this issue with the Russian side and as a result … we have a new mechanism … how to start a ceasefire, how to control a ceasefire. How to react for the violations of the agreement," Mr Lubinets told the ABC.
Land mines were cleared from the road leading into the city and weapons were laid down on both sides for 72 hours as 25 buses pulled in to evacuate those wanting to leave.
Mr Lubinets agreed to facilitate the efforts alongside his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, but he had to comply with Moscow's rules.
From the moment he entered Belarus, which is sometimes described as a Kremlin puppet state, he had to turn off all communication with the outside world.
Moscow limited his delegation to his deputy and chief advisor.
After tense negotiations, he was allowed to take along two Ukrainian journalists.
The whole time he feared there could be some sort of "accident" along the way and couldn't shake the thought that Russia was preparing something hostile.
Once they arrived in Oleshky, he was finally allowed to communicate with colleagues in Kyiv. His team fired up their portable internet satellite and beamed a signal back home.
"All these three days I almost didn't sleep because, you know, when you wait for something to go wrong," he said.
Mr Lubinets said the delegation stuck together for safety and made sure they travelled on the bus carrying the small contingent of American journalists.
"For me, it was an additional mechanism of security for myself and our Ukrainian delegation and my colleagues," he said.
'Russia used this situation'
For almost a year leading up to this moment, Mr Lubinets had tried tirelessly to get Russia to agree to a humanitarian ceasefire in Oleshky.
Then in September after the UN General Assembly in New York, he received a call from Melania Trump's executive advisor offering to help.
"He said that Melania Trump received information about Oleshky and she wants to establish the new format of negotiations with the Russian side," Mr Lubinets said.
Desperate for a breakthrough, he welcomed Ms Trump into the fold.

"Melania Trump coordinated us and suggested a lot of new initiatives. We had final difficulties, we solved it, we found a lot of new mechanisms, and we signed an agreement between Ukraine and Russia," Mr Lubinets said.
"I don't know if she has her own direct communication with Vladimir Putin or not … but I know that she sent several letters to the president of the Russian Federation.
"And we now have our special format of negotiations with the Russian side on the leadership and coordination role of Melania Trump. So, we will see."
All but 300 of the 2,000 residents in Oleshky decided to leave on the evacuation mission, which has been described as highly choreographed.
White House-friendly media outlet Newsmax was given exclusive television access while Moscow made sure it had plenty of state-aligned journalists on the ground.
Ukrainian media reported that ahead of the influx of journalists, Russian soldiers cleared the streets of dead bodies and rubbish.
"With me, were a lot of Russian journalists in Oleshky. Russia wanted to show to the world that Russia has a positive image of humanity," Mr Lubinets said.
"Russia used this situation. Russian propaganda tried to explain that in Oleshky we had humanitarian crisis because of the acts of the Ukrainian army, it's incredible."
According to some reports, more than 400 clips were distributed across Russian state TV and Telegram channels about the humanitarian efforts of the Kremlin.

Despite the deluge of propaganda, Mr Lubinets believes the mission has established a basis for negotiations going forward and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has identified a further 10 frontline cities and towns where he would like similar missions.

"I have communication with the Russian side; we have collaboration with the American side and on these formats we continue to negotiate for establishing next humanitarian missions," the ombudsman said.
"I really believe that this step that we've done in Oleshky can bring the real negotiation process and to bring peace to Ukraine," he said.

Aside from the Oleshky ceasefire, Melania Trump has been credited with successfully negotiating the return of more than 30 Ukrainian children Russia had illegally deported or transferred since the war started.
"I think that Melania Trump wants to do something concrete for the human dimension," Mr Lubinets said.
"To my mind, she doesn't want to spend time for discussions, for negotiations, for some procedure for the procedure. She always focuses for the concrete result."
